title: Tulip and Buttons' Surprise Party
markdown:
Beside a babbling brook, in a burrow as cosy as a warm hug, lived Tulip the bunny and Buttons the puppy. Tulip had fur the colour of dandelion fluff and whiskers that wiggled with every happy thought. Buttons was a bundle of wiggles, with ears that flopped when he ran and a tail that thumped a happy rhythm.

Their days were sunny naps, crunchy clover, and games of chase that ended in breathless piles of fur. Life went like rain on leaves. Soft. Steady. Known.

One bright morning, sunbeams painted gold on the burrow floor. Tulip’s nose twitched.

“Buttons,” she whispered, as soft as a wing on a petal, “Grandma Bear’s special day is coming. Let’s have a surprise tea party for her.”

Buttons bounced so hard his floppy ears flapped like little flags. “A tea party! With yummy things!”

The sun was climbing. If they wanted the nicest petals and the sweetest berries, they had to start now.

“We need the most special things,” said Tulip, with a determined wiggle of her nose. “The prettiest petals for cups and the sweetest berries for buns.”

With a hop and a tumble they went out into the bright morning. The meadow was green and dotted with flowers. The woods beyond whispered, and the air felt warm and welcoming.

“Look, Tulip,” yipped Buttons, pointing a clumsy paw at a patch of sunshine. “Big, sunny dandelions.”

They found the brightest yellow petals, so soft they felt like velvet against their noses. Perfect for tiny cheerful cups. Tulip held one up to the light. It made a little golden room on her paw. A butterfly with sparkly wings floated from flower to flower, and Tulip and Buttons giggled watching it, then forgot to giggle, then giggled again.

Then, tucked beneath a leafy bush, plump and round and glistening, were the juiciest red berries they had ever seen.

“We found them,” cheered Buttons, and he did a little dance that made his whole body wiggle.

They picked the berries carefully, one by one, so none would squash. Their paws filled with sweet fragrant treasure. Juice made a tiny red moon on Buttons’ nose. Petals for cups and berries for buns went into their little basket, and the basket smelled like a summer kitchen.

“Petals for cups, berries for buns, for Grandma Bear, the very best ones,” they sang together.

They carried the basket towards Grandma Bear’s favourite sunny clearing, the place always warmed by the afternoon sun. Arranging the party was the careful part. The petals wanted to curl. The berries wanted to roll. Buttons placed one bun, then another, then the last one, side by side, making sure each looked just right.

A small breeze tried to lift a petal cup. Tulip set a smooth pebble on the rim, just heavy enough, and the cup stayed. Buttons sat very still so his tail would not thump the berries away.

Then they waited. Fluffy bodies quiet. Ears perked.

Soon, with her familiar gentle tread, Grandma Bear ambled into the clearing. Her fur was the colour of warm earth. Her eyes widened, then crinkled into a smile that lit her whole face.

“Why, what is this?” she asked, her voice like warm honey on toast.

Tulip and Buttons presented their petal cups and their berry buns. Grandma Bear took a sip from a petal cup, then a careful bite of a bun.

“Oh, my dears,” she said. “These are the most wonderful treats. You are so thoughtful and clever to have made such a surprise.”

Tulip and Buttons beamed. Their shyness melted like snow in sunshine. They sat close on either side of Grandma Bear and shared the tea party while the trees leaned in, leafy and friendly. A bee came, looked, and went away again, as if it had been invited and then remembered another party.

Buttons’ tail thumped once, softly, against the grass. Tulip’s whiskers wiggled. The last berry bun sat waiting, and Grandma Bear split it into three.

The brook kept babbling. The petal cups kept their little yellow shape. And the two friends, who had always known how to chase and nap and munch, now knew how a basket felt when it was carried for someone else.
